nameStory: Nipplewort gets its memorable name from an old belief that its leaves, when crushed and applied as a poultice, could treat nursing mothers' sore nipples. This follows the medieval "Doctrine of Signatures" - the idea that plants resembling body parts could heal those parts. While modern medicine doesn't support this use, the name has stuck for centuries!
description: Nipplewort is a weedy annual herb that grows 1-4 feet tall with a branching, somewhat scraggly appearance. It produces clusters of small, bright yellow flowers that look like tiny dandelions but are much smaller - only about 1/2 inch across. The plant has an upright, somewhat gangly growth habit and can form loose colonies in disturbed areas. As a member of the sunflower family, it's related to daisies and asters but has a much more modest appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small bright yellow flower heads about 1/2 inch across with 8-15 narrow ray petals surrounding a yellow center. They're held in loose, branching clusters and close up in afternoon shade or on cloudy days.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lower leaves are deeply lobed with a large terminal lobe and smaller side lobes, resembling a fiddle or maple leaf. Upper leaves are smaller and less lobed. All leaves feel slightly rough and have a somewhat bitter, weedy smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a somewhat scraggly, branching herb 1-4 feet tall. Stems are hollow, ridged, and feel brittle when bent. The whole plant has an unkempt, weedy appearance.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, smooth, oval seeds develop in summer with no fluffy parachute (unlike dandelions). The dried flower heads become small, cup-like structures that hold the seeds.

habitat: Look for nipplewort in disturbed soils like roadsides, waste areas, gardens, and field edges throughout New England. It thrives in rich, moist soil but tolerates poor conditions too. Often found near human activity - around barns, compost piles, and anywhere the soil has been disturbed.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as rosettes with their characteristic lobed leaves. Early spring is when the distinctive fiddle-shaped lower leaves are most obvious before the plant starts branching.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time from June through August. The small yellow flowers open in morning sun but close by late afternoon. Seeds begin forming in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Plants continue flowering into early fall but become increasingly scraggly. Seeds ripen and disperse, and the whole plant begins to brown and die back.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, leaving only seeds in the soil. Look for dried, brittle stems and empty seed heads if the area hasn't been disturbed.

funFact: Nipplewort flowers have a built-in daily schedule - they open in the morning when pollinators are active but close every afternoon around 1-2 PM, earning them the folk name "noon flower" in some regions!
confusionNotes: The small yellow flowers might be confused with young dandelions, but nipplewort flowers are much smaller, grow in clusters rather than singly, and the plants have very different leaves - lobed and fiddle-shaped rather than the deeply toothed dandelion leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its unusual name, nipplewort is actually a European immigrant that's been naturalized in North America for centuries. It's sometimes considered a minor garden weed, but it's harmless and can actually attract beneficial insects to your yard.
compareHints: Nipplewort is the only species in its genus found in New England, making it unique among our local plants. Compared to other small yellow flowers in the sunflower family, it's distinguished by its combination of fiddle-shaped lower leaves, small clustered flowers that close in the afternoon, and its preference for disturbed soils around human activity.
